title: The Raven and the Goose
subtitle: A short story about colour and stubbornness

learningObjectives.text: What do the birds do to each other?

colours.author: Greenlandic storytellers, collected by Knud Rasmussen
colours.locator: The Raven And The Goose; The Raven And The Goose, normalized characters 144-698
colours.excerpt: It happened in the days when all the birds were getting their colours and the pattern in their coats. And the raven and the goose happened to meet, and they agreed to paint each other. The raven began, and painted the other black, with a nice white pattern showing between. The goose thought that very fine indeed, and began to do the same by the raven, painting it a coat exactly like its own. But then the raven fell into a rage, and declared the pattern was frightfully ugly, and the goose, offended at all the fuss, simply splashed it black all over.
colours.note: Verbatim English rendering by Worster from stories collected by Rasmussen in Greenland. The book title uses an outdated ethnonym; this lesson identifies the collection's Greenland scope.

narrativeBlocks.title: Two birds, one game
narrativeBlocks.body: In the beginning the Raven and the Goose are friends — or rivals in courtesy — and they agree to paint each other: each will make the other beautiful.

narrativeBlocks.title: The raven's careful work
narrativeBlocks.body: The Raven goes first and paints the goose beautifully — white body, patterned wings, elegant markings — the goose is delighted.

narrativeBlocks.title: The quarrel over the turn
narrativeBlocks.body: Then the goose takes the brush — but the raven is restless, quarrelsome, never satisfied with the work — and the goose loses patience mid-job.

narrativeBlocks.title: Splashed black all over
narrativeBlocks.body: The goose simply splashed the raven black all over — and flew away. That is why the raven wears black ever since: the job was left unfinished.

narrativeBlocks.title: A colour-origin tale
narrativeBlocks.body: The Greenland story is a colour-myth — the birds' quarrel explains the plumage we see: the goose well-painted, the raven's job abandoned in anger.
